title: AR Rahman Played Maa Tujhe Salaam at the India-Pakistan Border. Nobody Was Ready.
excerpt: The first-ever live performance at Attari kicked off the biggest Bollywood release week of the year — and early reviews are calling Main Vaapas Aaunga a masterpiece
body:
AR Rahman Played Maa Tujhe Salaam at the India-Pakistan Border. Nobody Was Ready.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=PRUTWluKRW8

AR Rahman stood at the India-Pakistan border on Sunday evening, the sun dropping behind the Attari gates, thousands of BSF jawans and visitors packed into JCP Stadium for the Beating Retreat ceremony — and played Maa Tujhe Salaam.

Nobody was ready for what that felt like.

The Oscar-winning composer's first-ever live performance at the Attari-Wagah border was organised by the team behind Main Vaapas Aaunga, Imtiaz Ali's Partition-era love story releasing this Thursday, June 12. It was supposed to be a promotional event. It became something else entirely — a moment so loaded with history, music, and raw emotion that everyone who was there is still talking about it.

The Set List That Broke the Border

Rahman opened with the devotional Chanda Suraj Lakhon Taare, his voice filling the stadium as the flag ceremony wound down. Then the concert slipped into the musical world of the film: Nilanjana Ghosh and Vedang Raina performed Maskara, the track that's been climbing every streaming chart in India. Mohit Chauhan followed with Ishq Mastana — a jazz-classical-Punjabi folk fusion that sounds like something Rahman should have composed decades ago and somehow saved for this exact moment.

The finale was inevitable and devastating. Maa Tujhe Salaam — Rahman's 1997 anthem that has, for three decades, been India's unofficial second national anthem — echoed off the border walls where soldiers stand guard every day. The stadium erupted.

"This is such a unique event. No artist has ever performed at the Attari Gate. It is magical that this is happening around Main Vaapas Aaunga, a film that originates from the making of the border during Partition. Not only homes and lives were lost, but hearts were broken as well. We bring a message of love because, ultimately, only love sustains us." — Imtiaz Ali

This wasn't just an album launch at a five-star hotel. It was an artist performing a song about loving your country at the exact line where your country ends and another begins — while promoting a film about the people who were torn apart when that line was drawn. The symbolism was staggering.

For the Indian diaspora, this performance resonates deeply. Many NRIs maintain strong emotional ties to their homeland, and events like this serve as a poignant reminder of their roots. The performance not only highlights cultural connections but also reinforces the importance of remittances and family ties that bind Indians abroad to their homeland.

The Reviews Are Coming In — And They're Glowing

Even before the film opens to the public on Thursday, the industry has started weighing in after special screenings. The word is overwhelmingly good.

Kabir Khan called it "a very moving film" that feels "relevant in the world we are living in," adding that he needed to "sleep over it" before he could fully process what he'd watched. Sunidhi Chauhan praised the experience as something entirely new. Ektaa Kapoor wrote that it's "emotional, timeless, and stays with you long after it ends." Aaliyah Kashyap — who'd already seen it once — watched it a second time and called it "hard-hitting" and "important."

When Kabir Khan says he needs to sleep on a film before talking about it, you're not watching a regular release. You're watching something that gets under the skin.

North America Cannot Wait

Here's the detail that has the distribution world buzzing: exhibitors in the US and Canada pushed to open advance bookings on June 5 — a full week before release. Imtiaz Ali himself said he'd never heard of anything like it in his career.

"This is unprecedented. I've never heard of such a thing coming from cinema theatres in North America — in Canada and in America — to advance the advance booking. My distribution team is very chuffed about it." — Imtiaz Ali

For the Indian diaspora, this is the film that's been designed with you in mind. A Partition love story scored by A.R. Rahman, starring Diljit Dosanjh fresh off his global concert domination, Naseeruddin Shah, Vedang Raina, and Sharvari — set across two timelines connected by the love that outlasted the border. This connection to the film is particularly significant for NRIs, who often seek narratives that reflect their experiences and heritage.

The Fever You Didn't Know About

Choreographer Ashley Lobo revealed that Vedang Raina shot the Ishq Mastana sequence with a 101-degree fever — and nobody on set knew. "It never reflected in his work, attitude, or energy," Lobo said. "His ability to learn, adapt, and perform with such ease was truly impressive."

That kind of commitment is why the industry is betting big on Raina. Between The Archies, his casting opposite Alia Bhatt in Alpha, and now this, the 24-year-old is building a career at a pace that most actors twice his age would envy.

Main Vaapas Aaunga opens in theatres June 12. In India, the UK, the US, and Canada. The music is already everywhere. After Attari, so is the feeling.
author: Diaspora Desk
